kaigo-atomic-immunity.heading: Immunity and habits: keep infection precautions
paragraphs: Immunity protects the body against pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. People who look healthy still face infection risks, so continue hand hygiene, clean–dirty separation and other necessary precautions.

The textbook discusses immunity in relation to balanced meals, suitable exercise, rest, sleep and mental state. Overwork, excessive exercise, insufficient sleep and prolonged stress matter for maintaining health. Consider support suited to the person, including age and existing conditions.

Even where the textbook mentions laughter or warmth, do not promise that one action will improve immunity and prevent infection. One food or habit does not replace precautions. Do not recommend excessive heating or burdensome activities in the name of warmth.

[Example created for learning] A colleague says, ‘They slept well, so let’s skip hand hygiene.’ Explain that good sleep and infection precautions serve different roles: support healthy habits while still taking precautions needed for the task.

kaigo-atomic-sleep.heading: Rest, body clock and sleep stages
paragraphs: Rest means reducing or stopping activity to relax mind and body. Sleep is not a synonym for rest; it involves sleep stages. Suitable rest and sleep support recovery, memory, emotions and physical and mental health.

The body clock contributes to sleep–wake rhythms over roughly a day. Morning light, brightness and darkness, and daytime routines provide adjustment cues. However, check history, condition and habits rather than imposing bedtime or waking time from age alone.

Non-REM and REM sleep recur during sleep. Non-REM includes light through deep stages; treating all of it as deep sleep is inaccurate. REM involves rapid eye movements and brain activity resembling wakefulness, but is not the same as being awake.

Dreams occur frequently during REM, but dreams alone do not identify the stage. The textbook’s brief phrase that the brain is not asleep does not mean REM is wakefulness. Appearance or one picture also cannot identify REM versus non-REM.

With age, deep sleep may decrease and sleep duration or nighttime awakenings may change. Individual differences matter; check each person’s nighttime urination or noise-related waking. Do not dismiss problems affecting life as inevitable aging.

Sleep records separate the person’s own words, waking times, surrounding noise or lighting and daytime effects. Tell the person responsible about changes from usual and discuss suitable rest and surroundings. Sleep knowledge alone does not authorize medication choices or diagnoses of disease or sleep stage.

kaigo-atomic-aging.heading: Compare aging changes with individual condition
paragraphs: Some aging processes affect everyone, but their degree and expression differ. Habits, health, historical context and surroundings contribute. Life stages such as infancy and early childhood, school age, youth, middle adulthood and older age do not determine one fixed ability for each person.

Losing previous abilities can bring anxiety or frustration. Bereavement and role changes may cause feelings of loss or helplessness. These can contribute to depression, so check emotional changes and daily-life effects. Listen to personal experience without assuming every older person has identical feelings or depression.

Changes can include difficulty hearing higher pitches, reduced vision or a narrower visual field. Check how the person sees and hears and choose suitable explanations and surroundings. Age alone does not justify uniformly shouting or taking over without asking wishes.

Reduced strength relates to falls; changes in taste, chewing and swallowing relate to eating. The textbook also covers reduced intestinal motility, kidney and urination changes, respiratory function and infection resistance, vessel-wall changes and tendencies toward higher pressure. Do not assume identical changes in everyone; compare toileting, breathing and circulation with personal baseline and actual observations.

Several illnesses may coexist, become chronic or involve complications. Typical symptoms can be less noticeable, so no fever does not establish that reduced appetite is only aging. The team checks overall information, including treatments and medication, without deciding causes from one symptom.

Dehydration, fever, constipation, swelling, insomnia, reduced function from inactivity and pressure injuries each need checking. Being seen in older people does not mean they may be ignored. Record feelings and changes and arrange necessary assessment.

kaigo-atomic-dehydration.heading: Dehydration: fluid intake, output and observation
paragraphs: Dehydration is insufficient water for the body’s needs. Consider intake from food and drinks and losses through urine, sweat and other routes. Besides reduced drinking, diarrhea, vomiting, fever and sweating can contribute.

Observe dry lips, mouth or skin and reduced urination frequency or amount. Pulse may be faster, pressure lower or temperature higher, but report numbers only as actual measurements. Do not invent values or dehydration severity from appearance.

Even if the person does not report thirst, check for changes in eating, drinking, excretion and physical condition. In hot surroundings and before or after exercise or bathing, review the room temperature and opportunities to take fluids according to the person’s plan.

If the person has fluid restrictions because of a heart or kidney condition, or has difficulty swallowing, care workers must not independently increase drinking amounts or change the way fluids are provided. Report a dry mouth or reduced urine output and request assessment. Follow the individual care plan confirmed with healthcare professionals. This lesson does not establish one fluid-replacement amount that applies to everyone.

Severe dehydration can threaten life and require medical care. Communicate symptoms and changes from usual and seek help through facility procedures according to urgency. Do not delay reporting because the person has not expressed thirst.

kaigo-atomic-fever-constipation.heading: Fever and constipation: distinct mechanisms and checks
paragraphs: The hypothalamus helps regulate temperature. Fever means higher temperature than usual and may relate to infection, inflammation or dehydration. Redness, fatigue or poor appetite may occur, but not necessarily together. Measure temperature and report it with usual values and circumstances.

For constipation, check hard stool, difficulty passing and incomplete emptying as well as reduced frequency. Reduced intestinal motility or muscle strength and delaying the urge can contribute. Compare with the usual pattern and record form, intervals and distress.

The textbook’s 24–72-hour description of food passing as stool is a reference range, not a rule that no bowel movement for 24 hours proves constipation. New abdominal pain, nausea or poor appetite can have other causes; report rather than deciding by days alone.

Meals containing dietary fiber, activity suited to the person and support at times when bowel movements may be easier, such as after meals, are matters to consider in the individual care plan. For fluids, also check swallowing ability and any restrictions. Do not impose the same meals or timing on everyone. When the person has a fever, confirm a suitable method for providing fluids as well.

Read the colon’s position in abdominal diagrams from the person’s right and left. Arrows help explain spatial relationships, not the force or repetitions for abdominal pressure. Check constipation support against condition and the individual care plan. Workers do not independently decide medication or abdominal procedures.

If bowel problems are accompanied by persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, blood in the stool or similar concerns, promptly seek help from healthcare professionals without waiting a set number of days. Actual assistance follows the person’s condition, individual care plan and facility procedures. This lesson is not intended to determine a diagnosis or treatment method.

kaigo-atomic-edema-itch.heading: Swelling and itching: observations versus assumed causes
paragraphs: Edema, also called swelling, is fluid accumulation in tissue. Heart or kidney function, nutrition, reduced leg strength or prolonged sitting may contribute. Weight gain can accompany it but does not establish a cause alone.

Observe the location, side and degree of swelling and any change from the person’s usual condition. Swelling may appear on the affected side in a person with hemiplegia, but do not assume that all swelling on one side is caused by paralysis. Include information required by the plan, such as body weight, in the report.

Exercise or elevating legs is assistance used when suited to personal condition and the individual care plan, not a universal treatment for swelling. Check with the person responsible about pain, new changes or unknown methods.

Itching can relate to dryness, temperature or humidity changes and clothing fabrics. Check redness, rash, affected area, severity and onset. Other causes, including infection, are possible; scratching alone does not diagnose a clothing allergy.

Communicate the person’s own words separately from the skin condition you have actually observed. Use moisturizing products and methods suited to the person and their plan. Coordinate with healthcare professionals if there are abnormalities. Do not add unconfirmed causes to the record or independently choose medication or a new procedure.

kaigo-atomic-insomnia.heading: Sleep concerns: patterns and daily-life effects
paragraphs: Difficulty falling asleep, waking during sleep and feeling unrefreshed are different concerns. Ask when they occur, whether they recur and how daytime sleepiness or activities are affected.

Irritability, fatigue or sluggishness may accompany sleep problems. Check daytime activities, feelings, light, sound, room conditions, pain and toileting needs. If the person reports waking to a corridor bell, record their words and time rather than substituting age as the sole cause.
Adapt morning light, manageable activity, rest and nighttime surroundings to habits and condition. Discuss long naps if they affect nighttime sleep; this does not mean banning naps for everyone.

Coordinate with healthcare professionals to assess sleep difficulty affecting daily life. Preserve observations and the person’s own words in records without independently choosing sleeping medication. Actual responses follow the individual care plan and facility procedures.

78.title: Immunity and habits: keep infection precautions
objectives: Distinguish links between immunity and habits from guaranteed infection prevention.
Explain necessary precautions even for people who look healthy.
78.context: Consider whether sleep or meal information is being used to justify skipping precautions. This is knowledge learning.
78.artCaption: Staff discuss meals and health. This does not illustrate infection prevention through one meal.

79.title: Rest, body clock and sleep stages
objectives: Distinguish rest, sleep, non-REM and REM and explain limits of a simple binary description.
Record waking conditions and the person’s own words and consult with individual differences in mind.
79.context: Check sleep concepts and read night records through established facts.
79.artCaption: This scene shows attending to the nighttime rest environment. The image cannot establish sleep stage or quality.

80.title: Compare aging changes with individual condition
objectives: Explain functional and emotional changes through individual differences and life history.
Consider atypical symptoms and multiple illnesses rather than explaining changes by age alone.
80.context: Distinguish aging tendencies from changes in the person before you.
80.artCaption: Listen to and record changes from usual without deciding causes from age alone.

81.title: Dehydration: fluid intake, output and observation
objectives: Explain fluid intake and output separately from observed and measured facts.
Respect individual conditions such as fluid restrictions and report changes suggesting dehydration.
81.context: When dry mouth and reduced urine are observed, check individual conditions without deciding a cause.
81.artCaption: Check fluids and personal sensations. This does not diagnose dehydration or prescribe intake amounts.

82.title: Fever and constipation: distinct mechanisms and checks
objectives: Explain fever and constipation through their different mechanisms and observations.
Do not diagnose from bowel-interval reference values; report symptoms and individual conditions.
82.context: Organize temperature and bowel information together with the usual pattern.
82.artCaption: Compare observations with records. Temperature and bowel-frequency results cannot be determined from the image.

83.title: Swelling and itching: observations versus assumed causes
objectives: Specifically report location, degree and change in swelling or itching.
Distinguish possible factors from diagnoses and consult without unplanned actions.
83.context: Organize skin observations and personal concerns and report without inventing causes.
83.artCaption: Report observations and the person’s own words to healthcare professionals. This does not illustrate the cause of swelling or itching.

84.title: Sleep concerns: patterns and daily-life effects
objectives: Listen separately to falling-asleep difficulty, awakenings and feeling unrefreshed.
Record surroundings and daily-life effects and arrange suitable adjustments or assessment.
84.context: Distinguish the person’s own words from environmental facts about nighttime waking.
84.artCaption: Discuss lighting, resting places and daily routines with the person. This does not establish a sleep-disorder diagnosis.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-immunity.prompt: Someone proposes skipping hand hygiene because the person slept well. Which explanation is appropriate?
options: Good sleep permits touching clean items with used gloves.
Eating well removes task-specific precautions.
If someone looks healthy, delay standard precautions until diagnosis.
Healthy habits and infection precautions serve different roles; continue necessary hand hygiene.
rationales: Good sleep does not clean the outside of used gloves.
Food supports health but does not replace precautions matching contact risks.
Standard precautions are not limited only to diagnosed people.
Value healthy habits while also maintaining precautions needed for the task.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-sleep.prompt: Why is ‘all non-REM sleep has one depth’ inaccurate?
options: Non-REM means being awake.
Non-REM ranges from light to deep, and sleep stages recur.
Nobody ever wakes during non-REM.
REM is identical to wakefulness.
rationales: Non-REM is sleep, not wakefulness.
It includes stages that one depth label cannot fully describe.
Waking varies with people and surroundings; absence cannot be guaranteed.
Active brain function during REM does not mean the person is awake.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-aging.prompt: Food intake decreased from usual, but fever is not confirmed. May age alone be called the cause?
options: Check and report changes and personal feelings without deciding causes from age or fever status alone.
No fever always means aging alone.
New poor appetite in older people needs no record.
Reduced intake alone establishes a particular disease.
rationales: Symptoms can be atypical; use actual changes to seek assessment.
No fever does not rule out other problems.
Record changes from usual regardless of age.
Report facts rather than diagnosing from one change.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dehydration.prompt: Dry mouth and reduced urine are observed, and a fluid-restriction plan exists. What is appropriate?
options: Do not report unless thirst is expressed.
Diagnose dehydration and independently remove restrictions.
Report changes and individual conditions, request assessment and follow the confirmed plan.
Give identical water amounts to everyone with these symptoms.
rationales: Observed changes need communicating even without reported thirst.
Do not diagnose or change restrictions from symptoms alone; contact healthcare professionals.
Report observations and check a method matching restrictions, swallowing ability and other individual conditions.
Amounts and methods vary, and fluid restrictions must be checked.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-fever-constipat.prompt: No bowel movement for 24 hours was called definite constipation. Which review is appropriate?
options: Use the textbook’s 24–72 hours as a universal diagnostic rule.
Check usual intervals, stool form, difficulty and distress without diagnosing from reference times alone.
Consider only days, without asking abdominal pain or nausea.
Increase medication until stool passes without assessment.
rationales: The transit-time example is not a universal constipation criterion.
Check habits and several symptoms and arrange assessment as needed.
Pain and nausea also matter; days alone are insufficient.
Do not change medication independently; report and confirm instructions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-edema-itch.prompt: Repeated arm scratching was immediately recorded as clothing allergy. What should be reviewed?
options: Scratching excludes infection-related causes.
Clothing color establishes the disease.
Omit skin observation if the person says nothing.
Record itch location and timing and observed skin facts; keep cause unknown and seek assessment.
rationales: Itching has several causes, including possible infection.
Color alone does not diagnose allergy or another cause.
The person’s own words and skin observations both matter.
Separate observations from assumed causes and coordinate necessary healthcare assessment.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-insomnia.prompt: The person says a corridor bell woke them. Which record and response are appropriate?
options: Diagnose age-related insomnia and omit the bell.
Ban everyone’s naps because they woke.
Preserve words, time and surroundings and discuss effects and adjustments.
Staff choose a sleeping medicine without checking causes.
rationales: Do not replace personal environmental information with an assumed age-related cause.
Rest and naps require personal adjustment, not a uniform ban.
This checks personal concerns, surroundings and daily-life effects separately.
Do not choose medication independently; arrange necessary assessment.
